# Semiconductors, p-n junction and transistor (`semiconductors_transistor`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/electricity.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Electricity & electronics (`electricity`)
- Deps: helped by crystal_detector, quantum_mechanics, vacuum_tube, semiconductor_purification, atomic_structure
- Core idea: Very pure germanium or silicon conducts poorly. A trace of an element with five outer electrons (phosphorus, arsenic, antimony), about one atom in ten million, adds free electrons (n-type); one with three (boron, gallium, indium) leaves holes that move like positive charges (p-type). Where p and n meet inside one crystal, current flows in one direction only (p-n junction). A bipolar junction transistor has two junctions back to back with a very thin middle layer, the base: a small current into the base lets a much larger current flow from emitter to collector, because carriers injected into a uniformly doped base diffuse across it before they recombine. It therefore amplifies and switches like a triode, with no heated filament, at a few volts, and can be made very small.
- Pitfalls:
  - Working with impure or polycrystalline material; grain boundaries and stray impurities kill the injected carriers, so single crystals of extreme purity are the precondition
  - A base that is too thick, so that the carriers recombine before they reach the collector
  - Staying with the 1947 point-contact form (two gold contacts 0.05 mm apart on germanium); it is noisy and erratic, and the junction transistor is the practical device
  - Staying with germanium: it fails above about 75 °C and has no stable oxide; silicon is harder to purify but is the material of the future
  - Telling it as a sudden flash; Lilienfeld patented a field-effect amplifier in 1926, and Bardeen and Brattain found the point-contact effect while studying why Shockley's field-effect design failed
- History: europe: 1874 – Braun's rectifying contacts; 1931 A. H. Wilson's band theory of semiconductors; 1938–1939 Schottky and Mott explain the rectifying barrier; 1948 Mataré and Welker build a point-contact 'transistron' independently in Paris; americas: 1926 – Lilienfeld files a patent for a field-effect device (never shown to work); 1940 Ohl at Bell Labs finds the p-n junction in a silicon ingot; December 1947 point-contact transistor (Bardeen and Brattain, Bell Labs), announced June 1948; January 1948 Shockley's junction transistor theory, working grown-junction device 1950–1951; 1954 silicon transistors (Tanenbaum at Bell Labs, Teal at Texas Instruments)
- Read:
  - John Bardeen & Walter H. Brattain, The Transistor, A Semi-Conductor Triode, Physical Review 74 (1948)
  - William Shockley, Electrons and Holes in Semiconductors (1950)
  - Michael Riordan & Lillian Hoddeson, Crystal Fire: The Birth of the Information Age (1997)
